BUILD.title: My school and local features
BUILD.objective: Name and locate my school and local features.
BUILD.unit: My local place and the wider world
BUILD.evidence: F: map check plus one independent location question.
success: Name my school in my chosen response mode.
Use a key to locate two features.
Show where one feature is in relation to the school.
BUILD.career: A school caretaker uses a site plan to locate places and guide visitors. Practise giving a visitor one clear direction.
words: find and show where something is
something you can identify in a place
a mark that stands for something
the way from one place to another
a short distance away in this plan
tasks: Name one place you recognise near school.
Choose one route and answer four retrieval questions.
Point to the school symbol using the key.
Watch how I locate the school and park.
Match each symbol to the feature it represents.
Watch how I describe a route from school to the library.
Choose the direction from school to the library.
Name your school and locate two nearby features on your own plan.
Show one feature in relation to the school.
next: Arrival: use the key beside the four questions.
Starter: model the school symbol again or add the park.
I Do: trace the school and park on the plan.
We Do: match the symbols together.
I Do 2: trace the school-to-library route.
We Do 2: choose a direction and explain it.
Independent: draw your school and nearby features.
Exit: check one location without the model.
Next lesson: use a simple map or plan of a familiar place.
models: I read the key: a square marked S stands for school. I find S at the lower left. The triangle marked P is the park at the upper left. The park is above the school on this plan. I use the symbol and position together.

I start at S, the school. I follow the dashed route to L, the library. I move right across the page. My direction is: “From school, go right to the library.” The plan is a teaching example, so it does not tell us a safe walking route outside.

supported: Which place is for learning: school or river?
The key says S = school. What does S mean?
Read or point to the words after the equals sign.
Point to the right side of this page.
An adult can model left, then you show the opposite side.
The right side of the page.
Choose a natural feature: river or library.
A river is flowing water; a library is built by people.
standard: Recall a place
Name a place people visit near a school.
Think of a park, library, shop or bus stop.
Accept a suitable local place; check the actual locality with the adult.
Read a key
Why does a map have a key?
Think about an unfamiliar symbol.
To explain what the symbols mean.
Choose direction
A library is on the right of a school on a plan. Which way would you point?
Keep the plan the same way up.
Right across the page.
Sort features
Which is human-made: a river or a bus stop?
Human-made means people built or arranged it.
Bus stop.
stretch: Choose evidence
How could you check the name of your school?
Think of a sign, school document or a trusted adult.
Read the school sign or confirm with a trusted adult.
Explain a key
Why can the same square mean different things on different maps?
Read each map’s own key.
Symbols depend on the key; do not assume their meaning.
Describe position
What must stay fixed when we say left or right on a plan?
Imagine turning the page upside down.
The orientation of the plan, or an agreed viewpoint.
Question a plan
Can a classroom plan prove a route is safe outside?
Think about roads, crossings and changes.
No. An adult must check the actual route and current conditions.

checks.question: Which symbol means park?
checks.feedback: The key shows P in a triangle for park. Read each map’s own key.

checks.question: From S to L, which direction crosses this page?
checks.feedback: The library is to the right of the school on this fixed plan.

independent: Name your school to the adult. Draw a school box. Add or point to two nearby features you know. Show one position with above, below, left or right. The adult may scribe your exact words.
Draw a simple plan of your school and two real nearby features. Add a key. Describe one feature’s position using left, right, near or far. Tell the adult which detail needs checking.

Draw and label a school plan with three local features and a key. Explain one position and how you would check it against the real place. Explain why this plan alone cannot confirm a safe walking route.
exit: On the teaching plan, point to the park in relation to the school.
The park is above the school on the page. Accept pointing or a directed adult response.
Name your school and describe where one real feature is on your plan.
School name and one plausible relative position, checked by the adult against the local setting.
Explain how the key and a position word together help someone find a feature.
The key identifies the feature; a position word tells the reader where to look.
BUILD.misconception: A map is a view from above, not a picture of the front of a building. Keep the page orientation fixed before using left and right.
BUILD.prep: Before teaching, confirm the school name and two familiar nearby features. Use the school’s approved local plan if available; otherwise make a shared plan from the classroom viewpoint. Do not ask for home addresses. The supplied fictional plan is for modelling; the independent response must transfer to the pupil’s actual school.
sources: Map skills context. Our S/P/L plan and symbols are original teaching graphics, not OS symbols.
Fictional diagram. No scale, real school location or safe route is asserted.

GROW.title: My place, the UK and the wider world
GROW.objective: Locate my place the UK and the wider world on maps.
GROW.unit: My place and the wider world
GROW.evidence: F: map-skills check and independent location/pattern question.
success: Locate the UK in Europe on a world map.
Explain what changes when a map shows a wider area.
GROW.career: A town planner uses maps at different scales to connect a local site with a region. Choose the map view that would help plan a local visit.
words: the relationship between map distance and real distance
an area with its own government; the UK is a country made up of four countries
one of Earth’s large land regions
say what is similar and different
tasks: Locate one place you already know on a map.
Choose one route and answer four retrieval questions.
Choose the view that could show a school entrance.
Watch how I move from Middlesbrough to the UK and Europe.
Locate Middlesbrough and the UK using the map views.
Watch how I explain the change from a local view to a world view.
Repair the statement about a country and a continent.
Locate your place, the UK and Europe and describe one change of scale.
Explain which map view you would use for a local visit.
next: Arrival: check the meanings of country and continent.
Starter: choose a map for a school entrance.
I Do: locate Middlesbrough, the UK and Europe.
We Do: practise locating the places.
I Do 2: compare detail in two map views.
We Do 2: correct a country/continent confusion.
Independent: locate places with the map key.
Exit: justify a map view for a local visit.
Next lesson: use atlases, grid references and digital maps.
models: I start with the local label: Middlesbrough. On the UK view its marker is in north-east England. I zoom out: the UK lies off the north-west coast of mainland Europe. Europe is a continent. England is one of the four countries of the UK; the UK is not a continent.

A local plan can show school entrances and nearby streets. A world map shows countries, continents and oceans but cannot show our school entrance at this size. When I show a wider area on the same size page, local detail becomes smaller. I choose the view to suit the question.

supported: Does a map help show places or tell the time?
Choose a country: England or Europe.
Choose a continent: Europe or Middlesbrough.
Which view could show a school gate: a local plan or a world map?
Look for the view of a smaller area.
standard: Locate
What does locate mean when reading a map?
Think find and show.
Find and show where a place is.
Country and continent
Is the UK a country or a continent?
Europe is the continent containing the UK.
A country made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Direction
What does north-east combine?
Use the two words in the direction.
North and east.
Scale choice
Why might a world map be unhelpful for finding a school entrance?
Think about how much local detail fits.
It covers a very large area so that local detail is too small.
stretch: Different views
Why could two maps of the same place look different?
Consider area shown, purpose and detail.
Different scales, purposes or selected features.
Parts of the UK
Name the four countries of the UK.
England is one; Northern Ireland is another.
England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Misconception
Correct: “Europe is another name for the UK.”
Use country and continent.
The UK is a country in Europe; Europe includes many countries.
Wider view
What happens to local detail when a larger area fits on the same page?
Think of zooming out.
Local detail becomes smaller and some is omitted.

checks.question: Where is Middlesbrough within England?
checks.feedback: The marker places Middlesbrough in north-east England.

checks.question: Which correction is accurate?
options: The UK is a continent in Europe.
The UK is a country in the continent of Europe.
Europe is a town in England.
checks.feedback: The UK is a country in Europe. Europe is the continent; Middlesbrough is a town in England.

independent: Point to Middlesbrough on the UK map and to the UK on the world map. Identify Europe. Complete aloud: “My place is in ___. The UK is in ___.” Use the labels or ask for an exact scribe.
Locate Middlesbrough, the UK and Europe on the supplied maps. Draw a small location chain. Write or say two sentences: where your place is and what changes when you zoom out.
Locate your place within England, the UK and Europe. Explain why a local plan is more useful than a world map for finding a school entrance. Identify one limitation of these simplified maps.
exit: Choose the view for a school entrance and name the continent containing the UK.
Explain why a local plan is useful for a school visit but a world map is useful for locating the UK.
Each shows the area and level of detail suited to the purpose.
Correct a country/continent confusion and explain one limitation of a simplified map.
The UK is a country in Europe; simplified maps omit detail and are not navigation instructions.
GROW.misconception: Europe is not the EU, and the UK is not a continent. This lesson locates geographical places; membership of a political organisation is a different question.
GROW.prep: Locate the school’s own locality with the group before the independent task. Middlesbrough is the worked Teesside example, not an assertion that every pupil lives there. Use the map marker, key and compass together. No home address is requested.
sources: Public-domain coastline data; simplified equirectangular teaching maps generated from the supplied land geometry.
Map-skills context; labels, prompts and worked examples authored for this lesson.

LAUNCH.title: Resource use and climate evidence
LAUNCH.objective: Explain resource use and climate change using online data.
LAUNCH.evidence: F: source annotation, evidence selection and questioning.
success: Identify the source, date, unit and geographical scope of a dataset.
Use two figures to describe an emissions pattern.
Link resource use to climate change and state one limitation.
LAUNCH.career: A sustainability analyst checks data provenance before advising a council. Use a figure, a geographical boundary and a limitation to make your advice trustworthy.
words: something people use to meet a need
information used to support a claim
occurring within a defined territory; here, the UK
million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent; combines greenhouse gases using their warming effect
a reason evidence cannot answer every question
tasks: Name one resource used to provide energy.
Choose one route and answer four retrieval questions.
Identify what you would check before trusting an online chart.
Watch how I audit the source and describe the figures.
Choose the statement supported by the emissions dataset.
Watch how I link resource use, emissions and warming without overclaiming.
Repair an overclaim by adding a geographical limitation.
Explain resource use and climate change using two figures and one limitation.
Give one supported claim and one thing the dataset cannot tell us.
next: Arrival: check the meanings of resource, emissions and evidence.
Starter: choose a source check.
I Do: audit who, when, unit and scope.
We Do: select the claim supported by the figures.
I Do 2: connect fuel use to emissions and warming.
We Do 2: repair an overclaim.
Independent: build a claim with two figures and a limitation.
Exit: separate a supported claim from a missing answer.
Next lesson: evaluate responses to climate change.
models: Who: the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ). Published: 5 February 2026. Measure: net UK territorial greenhouse gas emissions, in MtCO₂e. The rounded totals fall from 384 in 2023 to 373 in 2024: a fall of 11 MtCO₂e, about 3%. This tells us about emissions inside the UK, not the world total.

People use fossil fuels for electricity, heat and transport. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to warming. DESNZ attributes much of the UK fall in 2024 to lower gas and coal use in electricity supply and industry. But this UK dataset alone cannot establish global temperature change or count all emissions linked to imported goods.

supported: Which is a fuel resource: coal or a chart title?
A fuel can be burned for energy.
Does emissions mean gases released or distances travelled?
Think about gases entering the atmosphere.
Compare the tens after the shared hundreds.
Which helps check online evidence: its author and date or only its colour?
Think about who made it and when.
standard: Resources
Name one fossil fuel used for energy.
Coal is one example.
Coal, oil or natural gas.
Evidence
Why record the date of an online dataset?
Figures may refer to earlier years or be revised.
To know the time period and which release is being used.
Calculate
Find the difference between 384 and 373.
Subtract 373 from 384.
Scope
Does a UK figure automatically describe the whole world?
Compare a country with the globe.
No; the geographical coverage differs.
stretch: Explain a link
How can burning a fossil fuel affect climate?
Connect combustion, greenhouse gases and warming.
It releases greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, which contribute to warming.
Audit
Name two checks before using a chart as evidence.
Consider author, date, units, scope and method.
Any two of author, date, unit, geographical scope or method.
Quantify
A value falls from 384 to 373. Estimate the percentage fall.
About 2.9%, or 3% rounded.
Limit a claim
Why does a fall in annual emissions not prove climate change has stopped?
Consider emissions still occurring, accumulated gases and global scope.
Annual emissions remain positive; greenhouse gases accumulate, and a UK series is not the global climate record.

checks.question: Which statement is supported by the rounded figures?
options: UK emissions fell by 11 MtCO₂e from 2023 to 2024.
The UK temperature fell by 11 degrees.
checks.feedback: 384 − 373 = 11 MtCO₂e. This is a UK emissions measure, not world emissions or temperature.

checks.question: Choose the sound limitation.
options: The figures include every imported product’s overseas emissions.
UK territorial totals do not count all overseas emissions linked to UK consumption.
A government source never has limitations.
checks.feedback: Territorial means inside the UK. Overseas supply-chain emissions associated with imported goods are outside this measure.

independent: Use the frame: “DESNZ reports UK territorial emissions of ___ in 2023 and ___ in 2024, measured in ___. Using less ___ can reduce emissions. Greenhouse gases contribute to ___. This dataset does not show ___.” Say it, write it or direct an exact scribe.

Write or present a short geographical explanation: identify the source and date; compare two figures; explain a resource-use link to emissions and climate change; end with one limitation of the dataset.

Evaluate the claim: “Falling UK emissions show resource choices can matter, but do not prove the climate problem is solved.” Use two figures, a causal explanation and a geographical limitation. Distinguish emissions from temperature.
exit: Give the 2024 UK total and one missing answer.
373 MtCO₂e, rounded; the table cannot give world emissions, local air quality or a temperature change.
Give one quantified pattern and one geographical limitation.
384 to 373 MtCO₂e from 2023 to 2024; territorial UK data omit overseas emissions from imported goods.
Explain why falling UK emissions and continuing global warming can both occur.
UK annual emissions still occur, gases accumulate, and the global climate is affected by emissions beyond the UK.
LAUNCH.misconception: A fall in emissions is not a fall of the same number of degrees. These are net annual UK territorial emissions, not atmospheric concentrations or the whole UK consumption footprint.
LAUNCH.prep: Use the embedded historical snapshot; pupils do not need live web access. Pre-teach MtCO₂e and territorial. Explain that the source uses rounded headline totals. Assess the pupil’s evidence and reasoning, never demand a personal political belief.
sources: DESNZ, Final UK greenhouse gas emissions statistics: 1990 to 2024

Statistical release, 5 February 2026, pages 1, 3, 6 and 13. Rounded headline net territorial totals: 1990 790, 2023 384, 2024 373 MtCO₂e. 1990 = 373 + stated fall of 417. Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0.
